description: We’re a student team interested in software, AI, simulation, games, and space. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we’re exploring an interactive mission-design game where players learn real engineering trade-offs involving fuel, mass, power, communications, budget, and orbital constraints. We’re looking for curious teammates interested in aerospace, astrophysics, data, 3D art, UI/UX, or game development.
summary:
Mission Architect is a browser game where you design and fly a crewed mission to the Moon. You choose a rocket (Light, Medium or Heavy), spacecraft modules, life support and radiation shielding, then plan the orbit and fly it in 3D. The game uses real NASA data: the Artemis II trajectory, which you can compare with your own flight; DONKI records of real solar storms that can hit during the trip; and the LRO color map of the Moon. Earth and the Moon are shown at real scale.

It turns mission planning into decisions with consequences. Too much mass, too little life support or a solar storm can end the flight. When it ends, a mission report explains the cause and what to change, with links to NASA sources, so players learn by redesigning and flying again.

Most people only see the launch of a Moon mission, not the trade-offs behind it. Here anyone can test those trade-offs, fail safely and understand real mission design, with no installation.
details:
What it does. The player builds a lunar mission from rocket modules, plans the trajectory, and flies it in a 3D environment. The simulation tracks mass, fuel, life support, radiation, cost and travel time. At the end, a report explains the result and while you are on the flight you get some quizzes and fun facts about space missions.

Real scale. Earth (6,371 km radius), the Moon (1,737 km) and the distance between them (384,400 km) are not shrunk.

Eclipses and weather. The player picks a date and time, and the Sun and Moon move to where they will be in real life (it's actual position). With that information you could for example see Eclipses come from astronomical formulas and look at them just by changing the date. There's different types of weather , it can be clear, cloudy, rain or storm with lightnings, and Earth has day and night cycle.

Artemis II comparison. The map draws the real Artemis II trajectory and the HUD compares the player's flight against it, maybe scalable for more missiosn.

Space weather. We can also simulate real solar storms from NASA DONKI dataset, which may affect the flight.

Learning. The mission report explains delta-v, translunar injection, heat shield, life support, radiation and solar storms, with a NASA source for each, we also teach by doing quizzes mid mission, as well as giving fun facts while you are travelling.

Impact. Most people never see how many constraints a Moon mission has. The game lets them find out by trying.

Tools. React, TypeScript, three.js, Blender for the 3D models, Firebase Hosting, claude and antigravity for coding, shaders and some 3D models and fish.audio for AI voice lines explaining the game, photoshop for drawing the AI characters.

Creativity. Instead of a static dashboard, the player learns through trial and error in one continuous world from launch pad weather to the Moon and back. Designs can fail for real reasons, with the rocket breaking apart on impact and a report showing how to prevent it in the future. It has Hand-drawn AI companions reacting with different emotions and voice lines, you can also answer mid-flight trivia to reforce knowledge and even learn new things with fun facts of other space missions, you can also compare your current trajectory with past mission trajectories in this case comparing with Artemis II.
